subject: On‑prem VPC: fencepost plan for control-plane / data-plane demarcation
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Danielle Reyes <danielle@arclight.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 1 Apr 2027 10:05:00 -0700
Subject: On‑prem VPC: fencepost plan for control-plane / data-plane demarcation

Hi Danielle —

Following our kickoff call last week, attached is a compact "fencepost" plan that sketches the proposed demarcation between Redwood's control plane and the customer data plane for your on‑prem VPC deployment. High level notes:

- Control plane (Redwood-managed): lives in a small, customer‑managed VPC subnet (labelled CP‑Mgmt) with a tightly curated set of egress rules and mutual TLS to the data plane.
- Data plane (Arclight): tenant runtime nodes remain in your on‑prem subnets and talk to CP over mTLS via a backstop gateway.
- Egress options: we can either use a dedicated NAT IP range per tenant (preferred for auditability) or a local egress proxy you control that can forward and terminate outbound traffic.

What I attached: 
- redwood_controlplane_vs_dataplane_v1.pdf — annotated control/data demarc diagram
- fencepost_subnet_map_v1.png — CIDR suggestions and route table snippets

Asks: 
1) Can you confirm whether Arclight prefers a single egress IP/WAN NAT per tenant, or if you require a proxied egress with header forwarding for observability?
2) Any constraints on allowed source ports from the data plane to CP (we default to 443, 8443, and 10255 for health/tracing)?
3) We'll need a 30‑minute call to finalize the runbook and agree on cert rotation windows — are you available Mon/Tue next week?

If anything in the diagrams looks off, flag it and Jonas/Kimberly will follow up with specifics.

Thanks —
Marissa
VP, Product Operations
Redwood Inference

From: Danielle Reyes <danielle@arclight.com>

Subject: Re: On‑prem VPC: fencepost plan for control-plane / data-plane demarcation

Thanks Marissa — this is really helpful. A few quick clarifying items from our infra team: 

- Egress: Our security policy prefers a single, well‑known NAT IP per tenant for upstream allowlists. We can run an internal proxy but prefer NAT when possible (simpler for our firewall rules). Can Redwood guarantee a stable source IP per tenant, or will it rotate?
- Ports: 443 is fine for most control plane traffic. We asked for 8443 historically for metrics ingestion; would you require 10255 as well or can health checks go over 8443/443?
- Logging: We need proof of path (TLS negotiation logs and connection metadata) for SOC2 evidence — can you provide a sample retention plan?

I attached our constraints doc for visibility. Also: if you can mark the exact subnets in the PNG with the proposed NAT egress, that will speed internal signoff.

Proposed time for the runbook walk: Tue Apr 5 11:00 PT — does that work for you?

Danielle
Head of Infrastructure Ops, Arclight Systems

From: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>
To: Danielle Reyes <danielle@arclight.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 2 Apr 2027 13:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: On‑prem VPC: fencepost plan for control-plane / data-plane demarcation

Danielle — quick technical answers and a few alternate patterns. Inline below.

> Our security policy prefers a single, well‑known NAT IP per tenant for upstream allowlists. Can Redwood guarantee a stable source IP per tenant, or will it rotate?

- We can support a stable egress IP in two ways: 1) Redwood deploys a per‑tenant NAT gateway on the customer edge (recommended), or 2) Redwood tunnels egress through a pinned carrier NAT we provide (less ideal for security reviews). Option 1 gives you a single, fixed public IP you control.

> Ports: 443 is fine... would you require 10255 as well or can health checks go over 8443/443?

- We can consolidate to 443/8443. 10255 is legacy and not required unless you want unencrypted health probes (we prefer not).

> Logging: We need proof of path (TLS negotiation logs and connection metadata) for SOC2 evidence — can you provide a sample retention plan?

- Yes. We keep connection metadata (src/dst IP, TLS version/cipher, time, bytes) for 90 days by default; we can extend to 1 year under an enterprise addendum. Sample retention matrix attached in the CP v2 PDF.

Other notes:
- Certs & rotation: we will use short‑lived mTLS certs (7–14 day rotation) backed by an automated provisioning API. We'll provide a cert‑rotation window that aligns with your maintenance windows.
- Fallback: If the backstop gateway is unreachable, runtime nodes will queue telemetry for up to 48 hours and retry over the same egress path.
- Subnets: suggested CP‑Mgmt /28 for control plane, and runtime /22 per tenant. See updated diagram at the link below (I updated the PNG to mark the NAT position).

Action items (owner):
- Jonas: attach updated diagram with NAT marked and a short runbook excerpt (done)
- Kimberly: prepare the SOC2 retention sample and evidence checklist (to attach)
- Danielle: confirm that single NAT IP meets internal firewall policy

Attachments: redwood_controlplane_vs_dataplane_v1.pdf (annotated CP v2 layer), fencepost_subnet_map_v1.png (NAT marked).

Jonas
Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference
